subsubtopic: CYPRUS ANVIL MINE IN FARO, YUKON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for years the Cyprus Anvil Mine in Faro, Yukon, was a mainstay of the territorial economy. Between 1970 and 1982, when it was in full production, the mine provided close to 700 jobs and represented about 40 per cent of the Yukon economy. In 1982, when metal prices fell, Dome Mines announced a shutdown at Faro. The Liberal Government of the day moved to soften the blow and helped finance a strip-mining project which employed 250 workers. This initiative helped keep the mine viable. With some urgent action by the present Government, it is still possible to prevent Faro, Yukon, from becoming another Schefferville.
The company which has agreed to buy the mine awaits certain Government decisions, lower power rates, and other financial considerations. The Yukon winter is fast approaching. The company's plans to resume mining and milling operations this year become less attainable with each day's delay. Negotiations with the smelters have to begin soon. The opportunity to reopen this mine will be lost unless decisions are made quickly.
The Government has hundreds of millions of dollars for bailing out badly managed banks. Reopening the Cyprus Anvil Mine means 500 jobs for Yukon. Yukon needs those jobs.

Mr. Speaker, every month in Guatemala 80 to 90 people disappear. The Group for Mutual Assistance for Families of the Disappeared, or GAM, seeks information on disappeared family members. However, in March, President Mejia Victores said: "To take steps toward the reappearance alive of the disappeared is a subversive act".
Subsequently, two of GAM's leaders were tortured and murdered. One had his chest and skull bashed in and his tongue removed. In the other case, the death squads pulled out the fingernails of a two-year-old child before murdering the child with his mother. In spite of such torture and intimidation, GAM persists in its demand that the Government account for the missing family members. Each Friday it holds a vigil for this purpose.
GAM worries that the November 3 election will lead to a situation even worse than that prevailing today. It fears the military might try to clean out the clandestine prisons before it transfers power. Alternatively, it fears the new administration might use the election to close the books on the problem of the disappeared and say: "That is a problem of the previous Government. It has nothing to do with us".
In the name of humanity and justice, GAM asks us to demand that the present Guatemalan Government give a full accounting of the disappeared people before the election.

subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF LAKELAND, MAN., POST OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the citizens of Lakeland, Manitoba, no longer have a post office as of September 27. Canada Post closed it down because costs exceeded revenues by less than $70 per week. I received notice of the closure on August 16, and I tried in vain to obtain a stay of execution so that I could study the situation fully. Canada Post told me that the people involved had been consulted and understood the closure. The people were told, not consulted, about the September closure, and they were told by three officials travelling in three separate cars, the cost of which could have kept their post office open for several weeks.
As of September 30, Lakeland people must travel as far as 30 miles to pick up their mail. "No problem", says Canada Post. "The people have to travel many miles to buy groceries anyway, so they can travel that far to get their mail". Does Canada Post use this same logic as it continues with free door-to-door delivery for millions of urban Canadians?
Customers in small towns and in the farm community are losing services at an alarming rate, while at the same time Canada Post continues with expensive delivery in our cities. I suggest that a modest user fee for door-to-door service should be instituted, perhaps the same amount that small-town people pay for post office box rentals.

October 11, 1985
I quote from a letter to me from Canada Post:
You can appreciate the difficulty of our decision in these situations, where we seek to maintain acceptable levels of service while at the same time reducing our deficit.
Acceptable levels of service are not being maintained, and rural Canadians are subsidizing city mail service as Canada Post takes the path of least resistance in deficit reduction.

Mr. Speaker, the constituents in my riding of Nunatsiaq are extremely concerned that discussions to date aiming for agreement on a political boundary have regrettably been inconclusive due to certain unacceptable preconditions set by the west.
The media have added fuel to the fire as in the case of the editor of the Edmonton Journal, through the CBC Northern Network, referring to the Nunavut Constitutional Conference as a "tin pot banana republic" run by "tin pot dictators". Canadians in the south are forced fed with trivia on what has been happening in Coppermine, such as the press being kicked out of strategy sessions. The reason why the press had been kicked out was because it has been doing all the negotiating for the Western Constitutional Forum.
The continued pressures of fast paced economic and social change in the Arctic regions dictate an urgent need for the creation of a new, more responsive and representative Government. A boundary which includes Beaufort and Kitikmeot regions is fundamental to the survival of the distinct Inuit people occupying the coastal Arctic who share a common culture and unique way of life with the eastern Arctic.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians tell me they are not particularly interested in tuna fish or speculation as to who might have said what to whom. Canadians gave the Government a mandate to deal with basic bread and butter economic issues: jobs, interest rates, and inflation. That is what they want to hear about.
In just one year, despite inheriting a mess of unprecedented magnitude, this Government has done more for economic renewal than any Government in history. In my Province of Saskatchewan 13,000 more people are employed. The unemployment rate is down to 6.8 per cent. Nationally, there are
300,000	more Canadians at work and 180,000 fewer unemployed. The jobless rate has fallen from 11.6 per cent to 10.1 per cent, the lowest since May of 1982. Housing starts are up 29 per cent, retail sales up 10 per cent, and new manufacturing orders are up 13 per cent.
The Bank of Canada rate on election day was 12.38 per cent and this week it stands at 8.85 per cent. That is the lowest level in seven years. The prime rate has fallen to 10 per cent. Inflation remains steady at or below 4 per cent, the lowest since 1971.

Is the Government planning to issue newly designed bank notes and, if so, on what dates?

The Bank of Canada, under Section 21 of its Act, has the responsibility of arranging for the issue of banknotes. The form and material of the notes are subject to the approval of the Minister of Finance. Four series of banknotes have been introduced since the Bank of Canada was established. These are dated 1935, 1937, 1954 and for the latest series, the various denominations have dates from 1969 through 1975, depending on the year that the particular denomination was printed for the first time. Two denominations of the current series, the $5 and the $20 notes, were revised in 1979.
The Bank of Canada maintains an extensive program of research into banknotes with a view to maintaining and improving upon the high standards of the banknote issue. In recent years this has involved work on such aspects of banknotes as additional anti-counterfeiting features, features to help the visually impaired and blind, and techniques to increase the durability of notes. This highly technical work takes considerable time and involves several stages of preparation and review before a final decision to produce a new series can be made.
Once a final decision has been made to introduce a new series, to circulate alongside existing banknotes, an announcement will be made which will explain the reasons for any changes in advance of issue. Also, all practical information, including information on timing, will be supplied to help Canadians become familiar with the new series.

My faith today in the parliamentary system has been somewhat restored. After 10 years of work on this issue, it would appear that we are getting through the last hurdle as far as the House of Commons is concerned. Today I ask Hon. Members to turn their attention again to Bill C-73, an Act to validate the condominium ordinances of the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories. It is a matter of serious concern to the residents and the Governments of these two northern Territories. Following second reading on September 26, the Bill was referred to the special parliamentary legislative Committee, which reported it back to

the House on October 7. The Bill now has the unanimous support of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the special parliamentary legislative committee. For this support I am grateful, since it confirms my belief and feeling that this legislation is truly required and will be a benefit and a convenience for those people who have chosen to make Canada's North their home; those who have made a commitment to that part of Canada which, to be honest, requires in many ways a higher degree of willingness to accept the challenges of nature, location and geography than in the other areas of our great country.
Today I do not intend to belabour the facts giving rise to the Bill-the extreme housing shortages in parts of the North, the desire of the people there for affordable housing which they can call their own and the deficiencies of the Land Titles Act with respect to condominiums. These were well covered at second reading. However, I will address myself to certain concerns raised by Hon. Members which, while somewhat peripheral to the technical aspects of the Bill, have a certain relevance.
The Hon. I assure the Hon. Member that the Minister shall express his concern on this point to the Governments of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. It must be emphasized, however, that this is a matter entirely within the legislative prerogatives of those Governments and that the ordinances are territorial ordinances. It would not be in the interests of the Government, as a condition of introducing and supporting the Bill, to dictate to those Governments the terms and conditions which they must place in their own legislation. They are freely elected representatives of the people of the Territories, and I can assume nothing else but that their only concern is the well-being of the people they represent. This viewpoint represents not only the constitutional position of the territorial Governments but the sincere commitment of the Government of Canada to the devolution of powers and responsibilities to the territorial Governments and the people they represent.

speechtext: This is an important speech we are going to hear now.

This is an important speech.
This matter has been contemplated for a long while and before making any comments on the Bill itself I think it would be appropriate for me to recognize the hard work of the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). He introduced a Bill on this very same matter and the House saw fit to refer the subject matter of that Bill to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
In the standing committee the result of the deliberation on that Bill was to bring forth a unanimous recommendation that the Government act post haste to validate a territorial ordinance which was designed to ease the serious accommodation shortage in the Northwest Territories, and particularly in the City of Yellowknife where, according to testimony that the committee received from the mayor of that city, there is today
a zero per cent vacancy rate. We were all alarmed and shocked by the rising costs of accommodation in that city.
I think the standing committee also deserves credit for the manner in which it acted. It acted with dispatch. It endorsed federal action and did so last May 28. The only thing that is surprising to me is that an uncomplicated Bill such as this, dealing with a technical matter, was not dealt with before the summer recess. This resulted in a loss of the advantage of the summer construction season, and that is certainly very regrettable. The Government knew that this Bill had unanimous support, and that a genuine, demonstrated need existed. It is very difficult for parliamentarians-and I know the Member for Western Arctic is equally frustrated-to understand why winter will be approaching before this Bill is passed. I do not think we can now expect to see the necessary construction beginning until late spring.
In giving our thanks it is probably also correct to thank the legislative committee for the way in which it handled this matter so quickly, under the able chairmanship of my good and honourable friend, the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer (Mr. Isabelle).
Before resuming my seat let me just place this Bill in some context so that all Hon. Members will know and the citizens of Canada will understand what we are doing and why we are doing it. All the property registration in the two Territories north of 60 is governed by a federal statute which is called the Land Titles Act. That Act goes back to 1894. Of course, in 1894 parliamentarians in this House of Commons did not foresee or envisage something called condominiums.
It was in the late 1960s that the two territorial Legislative Assemblies passed ordinances to register condominiums. Having done so, they were advised that they were probably in conflict with the federal statute, the Land Tittles Act. When northerners talk about the continuation of a colonial regime, this could be cited as an example. Life north of 60 is still extensively and rigidly governed by Ottawa and this creates a great deal of resentment and frustration among northerners. We who have been members of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development for many years have heard recitations of this hostility and this frustration repeated over and over again. Yet so little seems to be happening in recognizing the capabilities and the responsibilities of northerners to manage and direct their own affairs. They really do not need Ottawa breathing down their necks, looking over their shoulders and holding their hands. They can look after their affairs very well, and the Member for Western Arctic who served for a long period of time and with distinction in the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories knows that much better than I do. The previous Government did bring in a Bill to deal with this matter. It was going to repeal the whole of the Land Titles Act, and at first blush that seems to make eminently good sense. Again for reasons that Members of Parliament cannot understand that Bill died on the Order Paper. It was not passed.
The present Government received advice that it would probably be well to delay or postpone the repealing of the Land
October 11, 1985

Titles Act until there is a full settlement of the comprehensive aboriginal claims in the North. I really cannot argue with that.
It seems to make good sense. It was probably good advice that the Government received. But we do need to get on with the settlement of these outstanding aboriginal claims in the North.
Much in the way of development in northern Canada is being delayed because these aboriginal claims remain outstanding and unsettled. In fact the Macdonald Royal Commission drew attention to the fact that this matter should be dealt with as quickly as possible. The Minister, in recognition of this, is now trying to put together a new claims policy. He wants to take out some of the impediments in the former policy, which caused more settlements to be blocked than were allowed. Once those aboriginal claims are settled, then I think the door will be opened for what we call devolution. That simply means the transfer of powers and responsibilities from Ottawa to the two territorial Governments and their Legislative Assemblies in the North.
[DOT] (MIO)
I wish to refer to the MacDonald Commission again. The commission said that this process of devolution, this transfer of powers and responsibilities to the North, should get under way quickly and that all provincial-like powers should be transferred to the North within a period of five years. Again, I would like to tell my hon. friends how frustrating it has been for those of us who sit on the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development each year when we examine the Estimates. We have confirmation that the policy of devolution exists, not only with this Government but with the previous Government and with administrations before that. Yet, we ask: How much devolution has there been? The answer is: Precious little. The Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) can correct me if I am wrong but I think the last time some control was transferred it was over co-operatives and place names. It was something as small as that. More recently, there has been some transfer of responsibility over the forestry sector, which is encouraging. It can be seen how slowly things move.
We still have a very large Department in Ottawa of more than 800 person-years which is responsible in some way which is never very clear to anyone for administering the North from afar. All of these federal public servants in the northern development part of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development are stepping on the toes of territorial public servants who are every bit as competent as those here in Ottawa. It does not make one more competent to be a federal public servant. It does not mean that the federal public servant is one notch above provincial or territorial public servants. These public servants are stepping on the toes of territorial public servants. They are also bumping head-to-head with other federal public servants who are working vigorously on their own projects in the North. I am speaking of public servants from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Departments of the Environment, Energy, Mines and Resources and Transport Canada. Thus, if one visits the North it would be difficult to meet someone who is not some type of
Condominium Ordinance Validation Act public servant. In order to find a real northerner one has to search around.
There are so many public servants that certainly devolution ought to mean that responsibility of the northern development part of the Department could be easily and quickly transferred to the North. If the Government wishes to save some money, if it is really serious about cutting the deficit, then it should look very hard at the northern development part of that Department and reduce it significantly. It could be done without causing any hardship or any serious difficulty to anyone in the North of whom I am aware.
I would like to give one example of the problems that we seem to be having with the policy of devolution. A few years ago the standing committee established a subcommittee, as the Hon. Member for Western Arctic will remember since he served on it. He proved to be very helpful because of his engineering background. We looked at the Northern Canada Power Commission wanting to know whether or not we really needed a federal Crown Corporation to supervise the production and distribution of power in all of northern Canada. In a province such as Ontario there are municipalities that can quite ably handle the matter. We came to the conclusion that there could be territorial power commissions which could handle the matter quite well, provided there was some continuing transfer of funds to assist the power rates paid by those people who live in isolated areas and who rely upon diesel fuel for the generation of electrical power. That was our conclusion. It was a long time ago. At this moment 1 cannot remember the year we tabled the report in Parliament, but I know that the Northern Canada Power Commission still exists. It still has its headquarters in Edmonton and not in the real North, north of 60. So far nothing has happened but we all await some action.
I conclude by saying that it is my urgent hope that the legislation which is before us will make possible more affordable housing to residents of northern Canada. We recognize that a Bill such as the one before us can be handled competently by northern legislators who are responsible to their electorates. It is a small, technical matter for the Parliament of Canada to be dealing with. It is really an item which is not on the national agenda. However, it has important ramifications for the North, as we have been reminded by other speakers.
Once the Bill is passed, the territorial Governments will be able to proceed with legislation or ordinances which they passed some 15 years ago. Can we really comprehend that? Some 15 years ago they decided they should act and they have had to wait since that time to have certain ordinances validated by the Parliament of Canada. Does that not illustrate that it is time for Ottawa to let go and allow northerners to conduct and manage their own affairs?
The Minister has promised that there will be action with regard to devolution. We want to believe that. All members of the standing committee will want to see some real and concrete results during the lifetime of this Parliament. Those results will certainly have my full support.

October 11, 1985
Condominium Ordinance Validation Act

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in support of Bill C-73. I agree with the Hon. Members who spoke before me that it seems to be long overdue. That is to say, the people of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon decided 15 years ago through their legislators to have a condominium ordinance. It was in technical conflict with the Land Titles Act of the federal Government, which had been passed nearly a century before, before condominiums were even thought of. However, for whatever reason, it has taken 15 years to come this far in removing that technical barrier.
Like the previous speakers, I have not heard of anyone who opposes the principle of this Bill. However, there is a problem associated with it which is not a matter of principle. In fact, if this Bill does open the way for the creation of more housing in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon it will certainly be a useful Bill. I am not convinced that we will have any sudden action with respect to it. Perhaps some people will say there was a time five years ago which would have been more favourable. What I understand is taking place at least in some parts of the Territories, particularly in Yellowknife, is that there is not a good financial situation for building condominiums and, perhaps, for building anything. It is expensive to build in that part of the country. Much of the housing which is being built is being constructed with federal subsidies. I think these subsidies are right and necessary. Whether or not they will be available for condominiums is not yet clear to me. Other Hon. Members may have a better view with respect to that issue.
The irony is that very few people living in the Northwest Territories are likely to benefit from this legislation. The Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly), when he was speaking to this Bill on second reading, gave some of the recognized statistics with respect to the gross shortage of housing and the gross over-crowding among the Indian people of the Northwest Territories. Very few, if any, of those people will be in a position to buy a condominium. They are not likely to be seen as potential customers for those who would invest in building a condominium. There is probably a very small potential market for condominiums there and, from talking with some of the people in Yellowknife, my impression is that the market has been shrinking of late as opposed to expanding. So this Bill may not have an effect for several years and when it does have an effect, it is likely to be of no benefit at all to a very large number of the people in the North who badly need housing.
Condominium housing is not the solution for low income or moderate income people whether they live in the Northwest Territories or in Toronto. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands, mentioned on second reading, and I in fact had the opportunity to raise it in committee, that in Ontario we have had experience with condominium legislation. It was passed in the late 1960s, I am not sure whether it was 1967 or 1968, and was no doubt much like the condominium legislation in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. But we found that when things were going well and the
builders were building rental and condominium apartments, no serious squeeze was felt. But since the early 1970s, in many parts of southern Ontario, certainly from Windsor to Kingston, building has dried up, not totally, but the situation is serious, particularly with respect to the building of rental apartments. In fact, in the middle of 1972, there was a downturn of investment in rental apartments in southern Ontario. Rents started to shoot up shockingly and in 1973 and 1974, there were 25 per cent, 30 per cent, 45 per cent increases for little or no reason. The landlord perhaps put on a coat of paint and said he had to pay the cost of the paint. Nobody believed that. It was simply that the industry decided that there should be a shortage of rental accommodation and, therefore, landlords were able to force rents up exorbitantly. The result of that, of course, was that rent control, for the first time in anyone's memory, became a major election issue in the Ontario election of 1975. The reigning Government at that time said no to rent controls and continued to do so until the day after the election when it found itself to be a minority Government. We then got rent control in Ontario.
Now, of course, the industry would like to rewrite history. It tells us that the reason for the shortage of apartments is the rent control legislation, but in fact that is false. It is a complete reversal of the truth. The fact is that it was the shortage of apartments which forced the unusual step of rent control in peacetime. We had rent control in wartime and some people thought we would never see it in peacetime. But the industry forced it on us.
Because of the rent control situation there was pressure on some apartment owners to find a way out of this. They decided to convert their buildings into condominiums, sell them off and spend their money out west or in buying up Florida or New York, which some of the large real estate companies in Toronto are busy doing. The legislation in Ontario provides that the municipality shall have power to approve or disapprove, allow or disallow a conversion from a rental building to a condominium. Toronto City Council did exercise that power because of the great need of the people in Toronto for rental accommodation. Toronto adopted a policy statement that there should be no conversions from rental apartments to condominiums so long as the vacancy rate was below 2 per cent. It did make some exceptions. It said that if the rents are already so high that only the rich are renting, it might as well let the rich buy them if they want to. However, for most apartment buildings there was to be no conversions until the vacancy rate rose above 2 per cent. In the last 15 years that has never happened in Toronto.
On the basis of that experience, I would suggest that the Legislatures of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon take note of what has happened and guard against the loss of rental accommodation. I believe there are only about 504 rental units in the larger apartment buildings in the City of Yellowknife. Actually, there are 700 units publicly owned and leased, but only 500 units in the private market. I am sure it would be a great hardship for many people in Yellowknife if those 500 units were to be converted to condominiums. The Legislatures
October 11, 1985

have the power to prevent that. I believe the Legislature of the Northwest Territories is meeting next week. I do not know about the Legislature of the Yukon. In principle, the Legislatures have the power to prevent this conversion or, if they wish, they can share that power with the municipalities. But they should simply recognize that below a certain vacancy rate it is not in the public interest to eliminate rental accommodation. The vacancy rate in Yellowknife is worse, from a tenant's point of view, than the vacancy rate in Toronto has ever been. It is zero. There are no apartments to rent in Yellowknife so I have been told by knowledgeable people. This would be a poor time to turf out tenants because the owner wants to sell the apartment as a condominium and the tenant does not have the money to buy it.
I urge, therefore, the Legislatures of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories to profit from the experience in places like Toronto. In spite of the policy of the Ontario legislation, Toronto in 10 years or 15 years lost 1,800 rental units. Some of them were very expensive and, therefore, perhaps, it was no loss in a practical way. But some of them were units which had been rented to people who could not afford to buy them as condominiums. I believe the municipalities of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon should take warning from Toronto.
I agree with the two previous speakers and the Minister that this is a decision which belongs to the people in the Legislatures of the Territories. It is correct to pass this problem on to them as it is without attempting to amend it here. We should leave to them the responsibility to resolve that problem. However, I do recommend that they look at the experience not only of Toronto but in a good many other cities in the south where tenants have been very hard pressed by the loss of rental units. That being said, Mr. Speaker, I am happy to approve the legislation. I hope that the serious shortage of decent and affordable housing in the two Territories will be relieved.

October 11, 1985
The Governor General's Act THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S ACT

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
that Bill C-78, an Act to amend the Governor General's Act, the Governor General's Retiring Annuity Act, the Salaries Act and the Judges Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to commend to Members of this honourable House Bill C-78, an Act to amend the Governor General's Act, the Governor General's Retiring Annuity Act, the Salaries Act and the Judges Act. Just to start things off, the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) will not be speaking in this debate so I wish to touch first on the changes this Bill provides with reference to the emoluments of the Governor General and the Lieutenant-Governor. The salary of the Governor General of Canada was fixed at Confederation at 10,000 pounds sterling. In 1931 it was converted from sterling to $48,666.63 and has remained at that level until today. The salary is, however, tax-free. If this Bill is passed by the House, the Governor General's salary would be increased to $70,000, which I think is clearly more appropriate for the occupant of that office. In addition, there is a slight amendment to the Governor General's Retiring Annuity Act.
The Lieutenant-Governors have had their salaries revised by statute only three times since 1867; in 1952, 1975 and again in
1983.	Without going into too much detail, this Bill would increase the salary of all Lieutenant-Governors to $69,000 a year as of January 1, 1985. Their present salary is $44,100. However, those salaries are taxable rather than not taxable which is true of the Governor General. I think there will be no hesitation by Members of the House in approving these salary increases for both Her Excellency the Governor General and for the Lieutenant-Governors who today are, by and large, not persons of any substantial wealth and who therefore need to have a reasonable salary if they are to occupy those offices. Of course, that reminds me that the new Lieutenant-Governor of Ontario happens to be a former colleague of ours in the person of His Excellency Lincoln Alexander, so I hope Line will be pleased with this presentation I am making here today.
He wrote the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Just before getting into subject matter of the increases we propose for the judiciary, I want to outline the context within which the judiciary is operating in our system. We have had a very productive year in the area of justice, the most productive, I would say, in many years, since September,
1984.	This House passed Bill C-14, the Foreign Extraterritorial Measures Act. The Opposition when it was in Government had a similar Act lying around for several years but could do nothing with it. We have now passed that legislation, which puts Canada in a position where we have some weapons at our disposal to use if there are any threats to our sovereignty through interference with the operation of Canadian law
through another state such as the U.S. trying to apply its influence in an extraterritorial manner.
The House has also passed amendments with respect to the Ontario and Manitoba courts, namely, Bill C-3 and Bill C-61. We have made major amendments to the Criminal Code through the Criminal Law Amendment Act known as Bill C-18. That will be proclaimed on December 2 of this year. These are major amendments, particularly regarding impaired and drunken driving. That measure will be proclaimed three weeks ahead of the Christmas season. There will be an intense campaign to make the provisions of the Bill well known at the end of November, and of course there are a great many other amendments included in that legislation.
The House enacted the Charter Conformity Bill, which will be proclaimed on October 15. We prepared a discussion paper on equality. We appointed a subcommittee of the House Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs to consider this discussion paper on issues raised by the coming into force of the equality provisions of the Charter on April 17. That committee is going to report, I believe, on October 25. As a result of its report we will have to respond to its recommendations and findings. There will be another charter conformity Bill arising out of the subcommittee's report as soon as time permits it to be prepared.
Bills C-47 and C-48 are now before a committee of the House. They are the new Divorce Act and the Bill for family orders enforcement which are about to be studied at the clause by clause stage. I believe that those two pieces of legislation will have a greater effect on Canadian life than any other legislation which will be enacted in the House during this Parliament. This is not the time to go into the details, but the family orders enforcement Bill includes an effecitve national system for the enforcement of maintenance and custody orders, the lack of which has been a national scandal for some years.
Bill C-49 is legislation to deal with the problem of street soliciting and is now before a legislative committee and should be passed through the House before the end of November. That legislation deals with a major public nuisance and decaptures the streets of the cities of this country for the ordinary law-abiding citizen. That legislation deals with a problem which has existed since 1978 about which the predecessor Government dithered and twittered around and did nothing.
Bill C-78 deals with the issue of compensation for judges. Every three years there must be a report by an independent commission on what should be done about judges' compensation and emoluments. There was such a report produced over two years ago, about a year before the Official Opposition was defeated last year. Unfortunately, no effective action was taken and we are now dealing with that matter, the details of which I will give in a few moments.
In the area of justice, during the last year we have entered into a mutual legal assistance treaty with the United States in order that both countries can be more effective in attempting
October 11, 1985

to deal with crime and in assisting one another in the battle against crime. There will be legislation forthcoming in the House in the next few months for the implementation of that treaty. We have adopted a policy of compensation for wrongfully convicted and imprisoned persons. Our predecessor Government refused to deal with that problem. It refused to join with the provinces and the provinces were forced to compensate such persons on their own. The federal Government has paid half of the compensation which the Province of Nova Scotia agreed to pay to Mr. Marshall who was found to be wrongfully convicted and imprisoned. We have advised British Columbia that we will do the same in connection with the Fox case there.
There is before the House a resolution on reform of the Senate. As time permits, we will see what becomes of that. We have introduced a new policy in the Charter Challenges Program which was announced a week or two ago. It provides $9 million over the next three years to assist women, the handicapped, and other persons who may wish to take advantage of the equality clauses of the new Charter in worthy cases of national importance. Who is to be assisted and to what extent will be decided by a board of competent people independent of the Government.
We have established the Deschenes Commission to deal with the question of whether there are any war criminals or persons reasonably suspected of being war criminals in Canada today or whether there have been any such people here in the past. We have, therefore, taken some action on that very sore and important question as the commission is now sitting.
These are just some of the highlights of the actions taken on the justice scene in the last year. This is only a warm-up compared to what I hope to have before the House in the course of the next year.
We will have to deal with the question of the Constitution, pornography, hate literature, child abuse, the Badgely and Fraser Reports, and, hopefully, our response to those through legislation will be put before the House in the new year. I am ascribing a high priority to the question of mental disorder and the criminal law. This area badly needs reform. I intend to have legislation dealing with that subject before the House this fall. As 1 mentioned earlier, there will be another Charter conformity Bill and mutual legal assistance treaty legislation.
This fall most important legislation will be placed before the House dealing with the application of Canadian laws to the off-shore, the Off-shore Laws Extension Act. This is particularly important because of our determination to establish clearly the fact that Canada has sovereignty in the Arctic and northern regions of this country. For the first time in many years decisive action in that respect is being taken. There will be legislation coming before the House dealing with the implementation of the Atlantic Accord in the energy area between Canada and Newfoundland. There will be legislation forthcoming dealing with important amendments to the Supreme Court Act. There will be legislation proposed dealing with the question of tax appeals amending the Tax Court of Canada Act and the Income Tax Act.
The Governor General's Act
There will be Criminal Code amendments suggested, Mr. Speaker, in the area of contempt of court, the jury, theft and fraud, vandalism and arson, and dealing with the question of proceeds from crime. There will be a new Bill coming before the House in the next few months proposing amendments to the Federal Court Act and the Crown Liability Act.
I intend to assign a high priority to the question of changes in the process of the appointment of judges. We have had a report from a committee of the Canadian Bar Association which, of course, we will consider in the course of deciding how we are going to change the process to ensure that there are improvements in it. 1 also intend to deal with the question of judicial independence and the reports which have been made in that area in order that it be not only a fact that our judiciary is independent, but that it be apparent that we have an independent judiciary. There will be some changes in the criminal legal aid area and initiatives in the area of the victims of crime.
We will have to deal, of course, during the course of the next several years, with changes to the Constitution, particularly, hopefully, in connection with the endorsement of the Constitution by the Province of Quebec. There are amendments to be suggested in connection with Newfoundland Pentecostal schools. Of course, there will have to be changes in connection with aboriginal rights and it is very likely that changes will have to be considered in connection with the upper House.
This is the general context of the framework of the past 12 months in the field of justice and our prospects for the next several years. I am hoping that Members of the House will have an opportunity to deal with all of these matters in such a way that progress will be achieved in all areas within the next two years. If we can make progress at the rate of that achieved in the last year, it will certainly be an astonishing three years in the area of social justice.
This brings me to the subject of the judiciary. If we are to have social justice and if this framework is to work and these reforms are to be carried out satisfactorily, we must have an independent and able judiciary. We must have a judicial system which attracts people to become judges. As a matter of interest, Mr. Speaker, we have 793 Section 96 judges. That is, there are 793 federal judges appointed by the Government of Canada. Eighty-two of them are supernumerary judges and 711 are in the active category. Of course, the supernumerary judges hear cases as well, but not on a full-time basis. As another point of interest, I point out that since the Government took office it has made 68 new appointments, seven judges have been elevated to higher courts, and six have been transferred. The total number of appointments in the last year was 81. The total expenditure on salaries for our judges in the last fiscal year ending May 31, 1985, was $64,893,806.40. The total expenditure this year, if there are no changes based on the judges presently holding office, is projected to be $70,992,539.53. If this Bill is enacted, we would add $9,580,710 to salaries for the present fiscal year. There would be an increase of $136,000 for conference allowances and an increase of

$141,500 for the representation allowances. The increase in salaries and allowances would be $9,858,200.
It is interesting to note also that of the total number of judges, 231 are county or district judges and of the total number of judges as of September 1-this has changed slightly since then-41 are women. Obviously, there are too few female judges and this is an area to which we must and will give high priority. It is only being held back by the fact that women in large numbers have only joined the legal profession in the last 10 or 15 years. Since one must be in practice for at least 10 years before becoming a judge, this, at the moment, limits the number of available women to become judges. However, it is a high priority for us to increase the number of female judges in this country as rapidly as possible.
To operate this whole system we need judges who are intelligent, who have ability, who are hard working, independent and understanding. We need judges who are humane, literate, discerning and who are well disposed and humble. That is a great attribute of a judge. There are not too many humble judges but I strongly recommend it to members of the judiciary. They should be polite and caring. These are the kinds of judges that we want to encourage on the benches of our country. They will not be encouraged there unless we make sure that their working conditions and emoluments are attractive to them. Whether we like it or not, we must face the fact that lawyers can do very well in their own practices without going to the bench. In fact, those who are not failures-because there are always some failures in any profession-do much better by staying in private practice than they can ever do on the bench. When we consider what we pay judges, we must make the comparison to what they can earn in private life if we are to attract them to the bench. They have families and other needs to look after.
Go to the bench, John.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If I ever do go to the bench, it would be the great bench in the sky. Perhaps that is the only bench I will go to.
Let me give some details with respect to the judiciary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said to get the dolts off the bench.
The dolts out of the PMO.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Hon. Member had better watch it or I will call him and his Party une bande de cruches, which means, of
course, a bunch of dolts. It is not widely known that I am bilingual.
Unfortunately, we cannot delegate the task, and the Constitution imposes upon Parliament the duty to fix and provide the salaries, allowances and pensions of the federally appointed judiciary. It is a difficult duty. It may have seemed straightforward back in 1867, but it is a difficult task.
We must balance the needs and expectations of our judiciary with our own responsibility to see that the money of the taxpayers of Canada is used wisely and to the best effect. However, we are not allowed to pass this duty off to anyone else. By virtue of the wording of Section 100, it cannot be delegated to any other body. It is a duty that is often found to be embarrassing and distasteful to Parliament and members of the judiciary because it results in public debate upon the remuneration of men and women who may be subjected, as a result, to generalized abuse but who, by their offices, are denied the privilege of public reply. Our judges cannot reply themselves when they are criticized here or anywhere else. Therefore, it is my duty as Minister of Justice to attempt to act on their behalf and be a public voice for them.
The fact that all of this must be done by Parliament itself carries with it the danger of politicizing judicial compensation issues, and unless the levels of compensation are reviewed at regular intervals there is also the danger of inequity and unfairness to the judiciary if their salaries and benefits are permitted to fall behind on the basis of leading economic indicators.
There has been erosion in judicial salaries since 1981, when an indexing formula was first provided to cushion the effects of inflation between parliamentary reviews. As I mentioned earlier, there is provision now for triennial commissions to review the adequacy of judicial salaries and benefits.
Mr. Otto Lang, a former Liberal Minister of Justice, two years ago reported on judges' salaries and benefits and that report was tabled in Parliament. At its 1985 annual meeting, the Canadian Bar Association passed a resolution deploring the delay in dealing with the Lang Report and calling for its implementation forthwith. We regret the serious delay, but 1 believe that we did not cause it.
We also have a mandate for fiscal restraint and to protect the nation's economic interests. As a result of that mandate, we are not going to accept fully, at this time, the Lang Commission's recommendations. We have sought to arrive at salary levels which will adequately compensate the judiciary, while recognizing the fact that we are in a position of fiscal restraint and are attempting to achieve economic recovery. Incidentally, it is good to see from the economic figures announced today that there is a drop in the unemployment rate and a drop in the interest rate. We now have the lowest interest rate in seven years, I believe. We are on the road to economic recovery. When the froth of insidious suggestions and when the cesspool of slanderous imputations is removed from the surface of the House of Commons, we can see the real progress that is being made in this country in the last 12 months.
October 11, 1985

We were fortunate in the past to attract practitioners to the bench who considered the judicial appointments not only a great honour but also a public duty. Those appointees were usually senior lawyers. When they came to the bench they had wide experience and a mature and reflective outlook on legal and social issues. Those personages were usually financially secure and could leave the rigours of practice and its returns in favour for what was then a more sedate pace of life on the bench. However, believe me, the pace of life on the bench today is no longer sedate. It is not a sinecure to be appointed a judge. Everywhere I have gone in the country, judges are among the hardest working. It is not a holiday. It is not entering into a pleasant retirement. Joining the judiciary is entering into a life of rigorous work. The work that they do is of tremendous importance.
Now, with the Constitution and new Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the judges of this country are in the trenches when it comes to determining what kind of society we will have in the future. In the last three years we have transferred tremendous powers to them. Now we must make sure that we have people at the bench who are more than suited to exercise those tremendous powers over us and our descendants.
The judiciary is still dedicated to public service. I repeat that life on the bench is the same as an active practice with the bar. The case loads in all of our courts have increased dramatically. The trend since 1975 has been to appoint younger men and women. Throughout the first half of this century the average age at appointment was 55, but it has fallen to 49. Far more judges have been appointed in their late thirties or early forties.
Much of our success in making judicial appointments has come because we are trying to consult broadly within the legal and judicial communities in making the appointments. I have mentioned that we will be reviewing the judicial appointment process. I intend to recommend major changes. However, the responsibility for judicial appointments will still remain with the Government of Canada and we do not intend to delegate that responsibility to anyone else, no matter what reports come in from wherever recommending that. The process can certainly be improved, though. Of course, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has announced that he has asked me to review the process and to recommend changes.
There will be full consultations in connection with these proposed changes with provincial Attorneys General, Chief Justices, the Canadian Bar Association and other interested groups. The McKelvey Committee Report will be considered by the CDA at its winter council meeting in February.
It is obvious that we must have very high standards on the bench. Their position within our constitutional framework provides that members of the judiciary have a greater and greater influence on the lives of us all. They will determine the shape of our society for generations. If they are to carry out that great task, we have to ensure that they are adequately compensated for this onerous and essential duty.
The Governor General's Act
Judges are just as vulnerable to economic concerns as the rest of us. As the age of appointment has fallen, the men and women on the bench have become less concerned about the hereafter, the retirement package, and are more concerned with the here and now, their salaries. Because they are younger appointees, they do not have the financial resources behind them that would permit them the luxury of indifference to their cash flow. Younger judges have younger families and they have to make adequate provision for them. I am surprised by the number of people approached by me or on my behalf to become judges who have said no because they have children who are going to university or have other heavy responsibilities and do not feel that they can afford to sit on the bench.
I know judicial salaries are high by the standards of the average Canadian but they are not exceptional when measured against the professional incomes lawyers can expect to enjoy at the Bar and they are not even exceptional when measured against senior public sector salaries. One must have at least 10 years at the Bar to be appointed. Once one has 10 years at the Bar in private practice, one should be enjoying his or her best earning years. Therefore, judicial salaries must be appropriate to those circumstances.
The present salary of a provincial superior court judge, the judge with which we are most familiar, was $93,800 as of April 1, 1985. This Bill proposes to increase that salary to $105,000. The Lang Commission made its recommendation using 1975 salary levels for the judiciary, applying the full industrial composite index and allowing for a cap of 6 per cent and 5 per cent in 1983 and 1984. Following that formula, the salary recommended by the Commission would have come to $119,000. If we adjust its recommendation to take into account not the inflation it expected but the actual rate of change, then the salary in accordance with that formula would be $114,000. The salary that we are recommending is $9,000 less for a puisne superior court or supreme court judge than the recommendation of the Lang Commission.
As I said earlier, it is not possible for us to provide salaries in the order of these recommended by Mr. Lang at the present time. However, we know that compensation must be adjusted because we have to take into account the erosion of judicial salaries by inflation and other pressures since 1975. We consider the figure of $105,000 to be just and equitable in the circumstances. Whether or not the salaries we have proposed are adequate will be examined again next year because we have to appoint the next statutory review commission in 1986. By the way, the Commission will be asked to pay special attention to the question of what changes there should be made to judicial pensions.
The salary of $105,000 was determined by restoring the relativity that existed in 1975 between judicial salaries and those of the most senior classification of Deputy Ministers, the DM3 level. I do not want to deal with all of the salaries because we issued a release with all the details. However, the salary of the Chief Justice of Canada would be fixed at $135,000 under this Bill and other categories of the judiciary would be scaled downward accordingly.

With respect to county and district court judges, the Lang Commission recommended that the difference in salary between a county court judge and a superior court judge should not exceed $5,000. We have accepted that suggestion. There are four provinces in which there are still county and district courts, Ontario, Nova Scotia, British Columbia and Newfoundland. Since the jurisdiction of those courts is not that much different from the jurisdiction of superior courts, the present differential of $6,900 will be reduced to $5,000. Under this Bill, for example, a puisne district court judge or county court judge will receive $100,000 per year which, incidentally, is $14,000 less than that suggested by the Lang Commission. Of course, the chief justices will receive somewhat more than the puisne judges. A puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Canada will receive $124,200. As I said, a judge of a superior court will receive $105,000 and a judge of a county court will receive $100,000.
The Bill also deals with certain judicial allowances. A representational allowance is provided to chief justices and other senior judges to defray expenses incurred in hosting or attending functions of an official or semi-official nature in their capacity as heads of the court. That allowance is also provided to the puisne judges of the Supreme Court of Canada and to the senior judges of the Supreme Courts of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. We will double that allowance from its current levels to $10,000 for the Chief Justice of Canada, $7,000 for the Chief Justice of the Federal Court and the chief justices of each of the provinces and $5,000 for all other judges entitled to that benefit.
The Lang Commission had recommended that the ceiling on this allowance be removed and that all certified expenses be reimbursed. Rather than doing that, we are extending the benefit of this allowance in certain cases so that expenses incurred by spouses can be defrayed as well. We felt that when a chief justice attends a Government or other official function on behalf of the court, it is usually expected that he or she be accompanied by his or her spouse. At the present time, there is no authority for reimbursing expenses incurred by reason of attendance of spouses and we propose to permit reimbursement out of the representation allowance for such expenses. That, in my view, is only fair.
1 believe that spouses should not be forgotten, whether they are male or female, and I am pleased that we are making this change. By the way, several years ago a report pointed out that in the External Affairs Department, the wives of diplomats and the like should be paid a salary. That is a principle which 1 thought was a reasonable one in view of the kind of life they lead and the kind of work they do without pay at the present time. As part of that kind of experience-
What about Jane?

speechtext:
Yes, I believe Jane should be paid a high salary for travelling expenses. However, I have not had her at any staff meetings. I never know when she is going to barge in, mind you. I hope that she is not watching me.
The terms of the removal allowance will also be broadened by the Bill. There is now a removal allowance available to reimburse judges required to move their place of residence on appointment to the bench or when they are subsequently reassigned. We are going to extend that allowance to permit payment of such expenses in two special cases affecting the administration of justice in the north. If the Bill is passed by the House, a judge who resigns or retires from the Supreme Court of the Yukon or of the Northwest Territories-and I am glad to see that both Hon. Members are present this afternoon-and if it is the judge's wish to relocate in one of the 10 provinces, he will be paid a removal allowance which will cover reasonable moving and related expenses.
The same benefit will be extended to the surviving spouse and children of a northern judge who dies in office, if the judge's surviving dependants decide to relocate in one of the provinces. However, this benefit is conditional upon the judge having been appointed to a northern court while being a resident of one of the provinces. These amendments are proposed in recognition of the special circumstances which exist in the North.
Finally, the conference allowance will also be increased. That allowance is now based upon a multiplier of $350 per judge on a court, with a minimum per court of $3,000. The purpose of it is to meet expenses incurred by judges in attending conferences, meetings and seminars which promote efficiency or uniformity in the courts or improvements in the quality of judicial service in the courts. We are suggesting a new multiplier of $500 per judge, with a minimum of $5,000 per court, as a response to increased travel costs since the allowance was last adjusted. We are not proposing any change at this time to the conference allowance of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada, which will remain at $1,000 per judge.
We cannot over-emphasize the importance of the judiciary to our system. We must strive, not only to secure the best legal talent available for the bench, but to compensate our judges adequately for the enerous and vital tasks which they undertake on our behalf. We think that we are proposing a fair and equitable approach to the issue of judicial compensation and allowances. They may be less generous than many in the judiciary had hoped and less generous than those advocated by the Lang Commission, but I think there are valid reasons to say that it is not possible to implement the Commission's recommendations in full. Judges are subject to the same economic realities as you and I, Mr. Speaker. Within the limits imposed by the need for restraint, I think that these amendments will go a long way toward improving judicial remuneration and the quality of life on the bench. This is why I am happy to move the Bill today.
In conclusion, I should like to return to the kinds of characteristics we need in judges. We need intelligence and ability. They have to be hard working. We cannot have lazy louts on the bench any longer. They have to be independent and
October 11, 1985

understanding. They have to be humane, literate, discerning, well disposed and humble. By the way, this reminds me of myself. Perhaps I should go to the bench; perhaps that is the only solution. They have to be well disposed, humble, polite and caring. It is not easy to find people of that nature. I look upon our judges today, as a result of recent constitutional changes, as voyageurs-and I did not say voyeurs-in a new legal frontier, exploring the frontier of the Charter. I look upon them as the coureurs de bois, the people who portaged and explored Canada in canoes, people such as Radisson, Des Groseilliers and others. Our judges are penetrating unknown territory. It would be very unwise for us to have a short-sighted attitude and sound to the general public as if we are paying judges tremendous salaries-and I think they are tremendous salaries-or to arouse envy among the public. The comparison is to what they can make if they do not go on the bench. We want the best, we want more women and we want more representatives of ethnic communities on the bench. We want a good mixture on the bench for this exploration; they are the new voyageurs. Who knows how they will interpret the Charter of Rights and Freedoms or what they will think it means? If any of us have to come before a court, we will want to have the best on the bench, and we will only have the best on the bench if we not only respect them but pay them well.
I thank my hon. colleagues in the Official Opposition and in the New Democratic Party who I believe will co-operate in seeing that the Bill goes to committee relatively quickly, like sort of today or, if not, the next day. The legislation will make these payments retroactive to April 1, but I hope we will not keep the judiciary on tenterhooks for the next several months and that we will give reasonably swift treatment to the Bill which I commend to the House as being a reasonable compromise.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by admitting that I had underestimated the Minister. I came to the House today thinking that his remarks would perhaps take five minutes to make and knowing that the Bill was heading for the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and that we would be able to examine it further there. However, upon listening to the length of his speech, I reflected upon the fact that he came from Newfoundland. In Newfoundland they try to say things well and, by and large, they do so. I do not know if that is a total explanation of it. Also I recognized, as I listened to his speech, that he was bound to set the record straight, as he saw it, and to try to demonstrate the terrible record in the justice field of the former Government, as well as the excellent record of his own Government in the brief one year it has been in office. I do not want to take the bait on any of his misstatements, no doubt through a lack of full examination and study of the Liberal record. I commend the Liberal record to him. I have to say for my part that I am disappointed that few things have been done in the area of justice in the year. However, I welcome the things which have been done. They were mostly bits and pieces of Bills on the
The Governor General's Act
Order Paper which would have proceeded during the last Parliament if only the Opposition of that day had been as co-operative as the Opposition of this day is intending to be, certainly in relation to legislation which we started. I thought, as he continued on and on, that even a Minister wanting to set the record straight would not have taken that long to try to do it. Then we found out the real reason for the speech being what it was, and I guess the real reason was that Jane was listening. I am glad that the wife of the Minister takes a considerable interest in her husband's work to listen that long, it being that full of baloney and hot air. I certainly want Jane to know that I enjoy her husband's speeches very much and I enjoy his presence in the House. I hope he stays out of trouble long enough to bring in even a small proportion of the many good things not yet delivered but promised. I hope Esterelke is listening, by the way.
I have little to say on the subject of the piece of legislation before us. It is a Bill to raise salaries, pensions and other related benefits. I endorse fully what the Minister said about the importance of the bench to a society which is animated, as is ours, by the rule of law and which wants to give absolute reality to the rhetoric that emerges from the House about our commitment to a society where all citizens truly have access to the judicial process. We want good judges.
My friend has offered himself as a candidate for the bench today. I hope he will not go until a lot of that good legislation about which he talked is brought forward and is made into law. However, since he raised the subject, I want to add a note about a type of judge who is needed and was not mentioned by my hon. friend. The record of the last year shows a lack of sensitivity to this criterion. As the judicial arm of the public administration of Canada has gained more and more authority by the passage of laws which have been referred to it and by the passage, in particular, of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, in addition to all the fine qualities mentioned by the Minister, we should add a greater reflection in the bench of the population nature of society. For example, he spoke about women. I was disappointed to hear him say that he could not find many good women to appoint to the bench now. He explained that only lawyers can be appointed and far less than half the lawyers in the country today are women. I still think, in spite of what the Minister said, and my own experience is that women can now be found to be appointed to the bench. This ought to be a more positive goal of the Minister than he indicated.
I recently tabled a question on the Order Paper which I had hoped would be answered by today. I asked how many of the 68 judges named by this Government are women. The reason I asked the question is that my sense of it is that since the election there are fewer women appointed to the bench, in proportion, than there were. I am very proud that in the former Liberal Government a substantial proportion were women. I have asked for the actual facts and when they are available I think they will show a falling off of the appointment of women to the bench. The Minister says he is in favour
