of it. He says that he cannot find enough good candidates, and I think that he is wrong. I hope that he will take another look at it.
1 want to indicate that it is not only women who ought to be represented more on the bench. There are other groups in the country whose views ought to animate the judiciary in Canada. Minority groups have very proud and able lawyers among their communities who ought to be elevated to the bench as much as possible, as a priority, I am indicating, not just as a coincidence, in order to achieve a judiciary which truly comes from the people of Canada, in addition to having all of the other qualities my friend mentioned and with which I very much agree.
Mr. Speaker, I will reserve my comments about particular provisions until we reach committee. I can tell you that the Liberals will not hold up this Bill. We are in favour of this increase. We recognize and note that it is not everything that was recommended by the independent outsider who reviewed the qualifications for judges, but it is an improvement. My sense of it is that it is an improvement that will make it easier for good people to accept when they are invited to become judges. On this side of the House we are all in favour of that.
As I said it was a very long speech by the Minister. He covered a lot of subjects that I could challenge but that is almost always the case with that Minister when he is on his feet. So far as second reading is concerned, I will simply note on behalf of our Party our approval in principle of the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak on Bill C-78 which has as its primary objective a rather substantial increase in the salary of the federal judiciary. As well it would increase the salaries of the Governor General and the Lieutenant Governors of Canada.
I do not intend to comment with respect to the proposed increases in salary of the Governor General and the Lieutenant Governors as I understand that the last time those salaries were increased was back in the 1800s, and it is probably about time that we had another look at that. Certainly we on this side are not prepared to storm the barricades with respect to those proposals contained in the Bill.
I had the honour of taking part in a similar debate, that is with respect to judicial compensation, some four years ago. That was on what was then Bill C-34, at a time when rather substantial increases once again were being proposed in the salaries of members of the federal judiciary. The previous occasion on which salaries had been increased was in 1977.
In March of 1981 the approximately 750 federally appointed members of the judiciary, and here of course we are talking about country and district court judges in those provinces in which there still is a country and district court, I believe Ontario, British Columbia and Nova Scotia; Supreme Court judges; Court of Appeal judges; Federal Court; Federal Court of Appeal; the Tax Court and the highest court in Canada, the Supreme Court of Canada, a substantial pay raise which was in fact retroactive to April 1 of 1980.
At the same time as we passed that Bill there was provision made for annual cost of living increases which were based on a percentage. I believe there was a maximum of 7 per cent in the cost of living. Finally, that Bill made provision for an independent commission to study the whole range of compensation and benefits offered to members of the federal judiciary.
In 1983 the first such commission was appointed. It was chaired by a former Liberal Cabinet Minister, Otto Lang, former Minister of Justice in fact, and that committee met and recommended some very substantial increases in salaries for the federally appointed judiciary. They reported in October of 1983 and recommended salary increases ranging from 26 per cent to 36 per cent, very significant increases. At the same time they recommended eliminating any contributions by federally appointed judges to their very generous pension plan.
The question of contributions to their pension plans by federally appointed judges has been a sticky and controversial one and indeed in the previous Bill the Minister of Justice had proposed eliminating contributions by those judges to their pension plans. However, in the face of strong opposition from my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, as well as from the then Official Opposition, the Conservative Party, the Minister of Justice withdrew those provisions and appointed a special commission, as a bit of a face saving gesture, to look into that whole area.
The suggestion was made that somehow by requiring judges to contribute to their pension plan the way all other Canadians contribute to their pension plans we were in some way attacking the independence of the judiciary. I have the report of the special committee that looked into this whole question which was chaired by Mr. Jean de Grandpre and which included Mr. Jack Birkenshaw and Mr. Jack Munro. That report made an astonishing suggestion. They said, and I am quoting from the report:
-there exists a subtle but real relationship between the annuity benefits provided by law for the judges and the quality, competence and independence of the judiciary in Canada.
Clearly any such suggestion that the requirement for judges to contribute to their own pension plan is in some way linked to the independence of the judiciary is completely without foundation. I was pleased to note that even the report of the Lang Commission quickly put the lie to that particular suggestion. I quote again from the Lang Commission:
We do not consider the issue of contributions to annuities as in any way affecting the independence of the judiciary.
I suggest that that is certainly the only appropriate approach to that particular question.
I was pleased to note that despite the recommendatoin both of the de Granpre committee and the Lang Commission that they did not in fact include in this Bill provisions to elimiante contributions by federally appointed judges to their very generous pension plans.
I want to put the Government clearly on notice that our position on this issue remains the same today as it was four years ago. We will vigorously oppose any Bill which is brought forward to eliminate contributions by judges to their pension
October 11, 1985

plans. That is not to say, however, that there are not deficiencies in the current provisions for pension plans for members of the federal judiciary.
I will refer to the report of the Lang Commission which noted that it had been made aware of at least one recent case in which a judge, after holding an office for over 10 years but less than 15, had resigned his office and was thereby disentitled from receiving any benefit, apart from the return of his contributions. The Commission said that was unfair and we in this Party agree that it is unfair. It went on to recommend that a judge with no final qualification for retirement should be entitled to a partial annuity after completing 10 years of service on the bench. That is a recommendation which was repeated by the committee chaired by Louis-Philippe de Grandpre on the independence of the judiciary in Canada. That committee recommended, as the Lang Commission had done, that there should be changes made in the eligibility in vesting requirements for pensions of the members of the federal judiciary. I would note that one outstanding former judge and lawyer, a man who has contributed a great deal not only to the development of jurisprudence but to human rights in this country, and I am speaking of Thomas Berger, is one of those who is affected by this present inequity in the provisions for judges' pensions. I hope that the Government is prepared to move forward on an early basis to make the changes necessary in this particular area.
Parliament is called upon to consider the question of the level of judges' salaries by virtue of the provisions of the British North America Act. Section 100 of the BN A Act requires Parliament and no other body to establish the level of salaries, allowances and pensions of judges who are appointed by the federal Government. Those payments are established by way of amendments to the Judges Act which come before this House from time to time. I believe the time has come to consider seriously whether this is in fact the most appropriate way to approach the sensitive question of what is an appropriate level of judicial compensation. I suggest that the House of Commons Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs may want to consider the advisability of looking into other approaches to the method of fixing judicial compensation.
1 emphasize that the final decision with respect to the level of such compensation must clearly be made by Parliament. However, it may well be that there are other methods for arriving at an appropriate level of such compensation. For example, in the State of New South Wales in Australia there is a provision whereby an independent remuneration tribunal is empowered to address the issue of salaries for the judiciary, among other federally-appointed individuals. The tribunal reports to Parliament and unless there is a specific objection to its recommendations by 50 per cent of the Members of Parliament after the passage of a certain period of time the recommendations become law. That is the negative resolution means of proceeding. I suggest, without endorsing that particular proposal in any way, that the time has come for us to examine alternatives which remove the direct link between those of us
The Governor General's Act
in Parliament and the judiciary when it comes time to fix levels of salary.
I wish to make it clear that we reject the argument that it is necessary to substantially increase the level of salaries for federally-appointed judges in order to ensure that the best people are appointed to the bench. I suggest it is totally without foundation to advocate, as does the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie), that we increase the level of salaries in order that those people who are already making $150,000 or $200,000 would then be in a position to accept appointments to the bench. We do not want a bench which is appointed on the basis of those individuals who will accept a position which pays a great deal of money. In fact, even the report of the Canadian Bar Association on the independence of the judiciary, the committee to which I referred earlier chaired by Louis-Philippe de Grandpre, stated the following:
-it is neither necessary nor desirable to establish judicial salaries at such a level as to match the judges' earnings before appointment to the bench. The most obvious reason for this is that such a policy would tend to attract people to the bench for purely financial reasons. The sort of person who would accept a position on the bench because it paid well is not the sort of person who would make the best judge. Rather, the sort of person we would wish to see on the bench are those who appreciate the honour of being a judge and who see as part of their reward the satisfaction of serving society on the bench.
I suggest that is a more appropriate approach to the question of what is adequate judicial compensation. The suggestion that somehow the best people are those who are making the most money is one that we in the New Democratic Party reject. There are many outstanding members of the bar who, in fact, are making salaries well below those which are currently being paid to members of the federal judiciary. In looking at the level of judicial compensation we have to consider as well the fact that there is a very generous annuity plan which should be included in any assessment of the level of compensation. Lawyers who are working in the area of public interest advocacy, lawyers who do a great deal of legal aid work and those involved in poverty law are not necessarily the best paid. They do not make as much money as corporate lawyers, for example. Nor do they make as much money as tax lawyers. However, that does not mean they are not eminently qualified to serve on the bench of this country.
I would note as well that by this bench-mark, as suggested by the Minister of Justice, senior members of the bar would presumably be unwilling to serve in Parliament because we are paid even less than members of the federal judiciary. The suggestion that the quality of representation, either on the bench or in Parliament, is directly linked to the level of compensation is one which I find invidious and without any foundation in substance.
My colleague from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) asks why there are so many lawyers in Parliament. I think that that perhaps is a question he may want to address in the context of his speech.
Stanley Knowles, the former Member for Winnipeg North Centre, spoke in 1981 when a Bill dealing with judges' salaries was before Parliament. I think it is appropriate that 1 remind the House what Stanley Knowles had to say with respect to

judges' salaries. I might say that he said the same thing with respect to the salary of Members of Parliament. Stanley Knowles said this:
Most of our senior citizens, and this means most of the 2 million people over the age of 65, are struggling at or just below the poverty line. We have many others, particularly women, in the 55 to 65 age bracket, those unattached who would be well off if they could get up to the poverty line who are having a difficult time-
1 cannot bring myself to believe that it is the right thing in the face of these problems to keep on giving massive increases to those who are at the top-
I still think, if I may go back that far, that there was something to the idea in Edward Bellamy's "Looking Backward", who said that those who had to do the dirtiest and the meanest jobs should get paid more than those who had the privilege of doing the delightful and the enjoyable jobs.
There is considerable substance to what my good friend and former colleague Stanley Knowles had to say on the occasion of the debate on judges' salaries in 1981. There is a great deal of job satisfaction in the work of a federally-appointed judge. There can be no greater honour bestowed upon a member of the bar than to be called upon to serve as a member of the federal judiciary. I think that the level of status within the community, the degree of respect, as well as the existing salary levels are certainly adequate.
I would note as well that there is a built-in percentage increase already in the Judges Act. When we deal with percentage increases on salaries which are already up around $100,000 what we are doing is increasing the gap between rich and poor. At a time when the Government is talking about allocating scarce resources efficiently, I have to ask myself whether it is really appropriate for us symbolically, if in no other way, to add to the salaries of those who are already at the top at the same time as this Government is cutting back on family allowances. I have to question the priorities of a Government which is prepared to move forward in this way. I have to question the priorities of a Government which tables a Bill to substantially increase the salaries of federally appointed judges at the same time as it tables a Bill to remove full indexation of old age pensions, a proposal which was turned back only as a result of the collective will, determination and energy of senior citizens right across this country.
It is my view and that of my colleagues in the NDP that this is not the time for this increase. I emphasize again that we do not in any way dispute the vital role played by the judiciary in Canada. What we do question is whether it is necessary to significantly increase these salaries in order to attract the finest legal minds to the bench. The argument is made that senior lawyers are paid well in excess of what members of the federal judiciary are paid. In fact, the Lang Commission included a table in its report which would appear to document that. It noted, for example, in 1981 that the average income of a lawyer who had been practising for 10 years, in the third quartile of the profession, was $95,269. Certainly those lawyers are not underpaid by any stretch of the imagination. Once again we have to ask ourselves as a society whether it is not the case that the gap between rich and poor is too great, that it is too great between those who have and those who have not, and
whether we, as a society, should be moving to narrow those income inequities instead of broadening them as this Bill would do.
The Lang Commission as well made a rather sad plea on behalf of members of the federal judiciary. It said that for many judges, particularly those in the large urban centres, and in areas with a high cost of living, cash flow is an increasing problem. I think all of us will shed a tear or two for the federal members of the judiciary for whom cash flow is a problem when we note that the bottom salary of these individuals as of April 1 of this year was $86,900. I do not think we have to shed too many tears, although I am sure it must be a struggle for them to survive on $86,900 a year. I am sure the cash flow must be a difficult problem but I suggest there are literally millions of Canadians who are struggling to get by on salaries far below those suggested by the Lang Commission as inadequate. Indeed, the current level of salaries is from $86,900 for a judge of the County Court up to $117,800 for the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada. I suggest that range of salaries will not in any way lead to financial hardship. Quite frankly, it will not in any way act as a deterrent to those who generally want to serve on the bench. I suggest that if someone turns down an appointment to the bench because they are making $90,000 or $100,000 a year, we have to ask ourselves whether that is an individual we really want on the bench in Canada today. If someone is prepared to say no to a salary like that, despite the fact that the position itself brings honour and prestige and, indeed, is the pinnacle of any lawyer's career, do we really want him on the bench?
I would like to deal for a moment with another area of fundamental importance to this whole question. That is, the nature of the appointments process. Quite frankly, I would have hoped that, instead of bringing a Bill forward to deal with judges' salaries, this Government would have brought forward a Bill to deal with the question of the method of appointment of judges. The Canadian Bar Association recently issued a report called The Appointment of Judges in Canada. This excellent committee, chaired by Neil McKelvey, interviewed literally hundreds of people and came to the conclusion that there has been a long history of political patronage appointments to the bench by both major Parties in Canada. The committee noted that although there had been some commendable exceptions, the practice of appointing the Party faithful to the bench has been all too common. Those were the words of a reputable committee of the CBA which suggested very clearly that political patronage has played an excessive role in the appointment of members of the federal bench. It went on to add that that does not in any way mean that those who were appointed were incompetent because they happen to be of a particular political persuasion. However, what it does mean is that we are not appointing judges on the basis of quality and ability; we are appointing them on the basis of their political stripe.
The committee said that in the light of political appointments, continued public confidence in the integrity of the Canadian justice system cannot simply be assumed. There is
October 11, 1985

cynicism concerning the appointment of judges and this cynicism must be allayed if public confidence in the legal system is to be maintained. The committee went on to say that the process of the appointment of judges tended to vary widely from province to province. For example, in the Province of British Columbia, Quebec, the Ontario Court of Appeal and the High Court, the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon, political favouritism has not had a significant influence on appointments. Speaking as a Member of Parliament from British Columbia, certainly that has been my sense of the nature of appointments to the federal bench in British Columbia. Political appointments have not been a significant problem there, although there certainly have not been an excessive number of lawyers who happen to be New Democrats appointed to the bench. However, the committee goes on to note that in Alberta, Manitoba, Newfoundland and in Ontario county and district court appointments, political favouritism has been a significant but not dominant consideration. Finally, in the most damning portion of this report, the committee says that in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Saskatchewan, political favouritism has been a dominant, although not the sole, consideration. Most appointees have been active supporters of the Party in power. That is a pretty stinging indictment of the method of appointment of judges in Canada today. I suggest that rather than focusing on the level of salaries we should, as a Parliament, be looking very seriously at the mehthod of appointment. This is particularly important at a time when the role of the judiciary has been significantly enhanced. The Charter of Rights, of course, has been in effect since 1982. The equality rights section of the Charter has been in effect since April 17 of this year. Members of the federal judiciary are going to be called upon to make fundamental decisions which will in many cases shape the fabric of this nation in the future.
I suggest that to continue with a method of appointment of judges which is clearly flawed and, in too many instances, based on partisan political factors, does a great disservice to the people of Canada. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, as well, that we look very seriously at the recommendation made by the CBA for an independent appointments process. I happen to believe that we should not reject as quickly as they do the suggestion of a role for Parliament in scrutinizing appointments to the federal judiciary. A similar role was played by American legislators, elected representatives. I suggest that we want to look very carefully at the implications of that in the Canadian political and parliamentary context.
As the Canadian Bar noted, Mr. Speaker, the primary cause for concern, the support of a particular Party, is totally irrelevant to whether a person is qualified to be a judge. Another concern they noted is that where political favouritism exists, supporters of Opposition Parties are frequently not given serious consideration as candidates for the bench. Those who support no Party at all are also often excluded. They go on to suggest that the system may produce appointments of unqualified people, those whose only qualifications are frien-ship with the Party in power or one of its Ministers. They also
The Governor General's Act
suggest that even if political affiliation may be a minor consideration, patronage and judicial appointments can become a means of managing a political Party. Finally, they raise two other major concerns. Now that increasing numbers of Charter cases are coming before Canadian courts, some involving review of political decisions, and of course the Supreme Court of Canada has indeed held that Cabinet decisions can be reviewed, as in the cruise missile case, Governments might try to stack the courts with people of their own ideological persuasion in an effort to influence the outcome of decisions on contentious social issues. Finally, and this is a very important factor, even if political favouritism is reduced or eliminated in judicial appointments, if the public perceives that it exists, public confidence in the judicial system is effectively undermined. The committee goes on to make a number of suggestions for reform and I believe many of them should be looked at by the Government on a priority basis.
There are a number of other issues of concern with respect to the question of the judiciary in Canada. I was recently most disappointed with the decision of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to call upon a justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, Justice Willard Estey, to conduct the investigation into the Government's mishandling of the CCB and Northland Bank fiascos. I believe the Chief Justice of Canada, Brian Dickson, very clearly and eloquently urged the Government as recently as last month to be very cautious before calling upon judges to embark upon commissions of inquiry. At a time when the Supreme Court of Canada has a very heavy workload before it, I believe the Prime Minister made a serious mistake in taking away an albeit outstanding member of that bench and asking him to conduct this commission of inquiry. 1 hope the Government in future will heed the concern of the Chief Justice of Canada and others in not appointing such individuals. On this point I would note that the de Grandpre Commission on the independence of the judiciary was very clear and explicit. It said:
The Committee ... is not in favour of judges sitting on commissions of inquiry except in those cases where the nature of the matter under investigation makes the choice of a judge as commissioner particularly appropriate. Time spent away from the bench sitting on commissions of inquiry tends to reduce the independence of the individual judge involved and of the bench generally. The most obvious problem is the absence of the judge from the bench. A greater burden is placed on the other judges of a court when one is absent for a substantial period, and the work of the absent judge may suffer.
Therefore, I think this is an appropriate occasion to draw to the attention of the Government my concern about weakening the bench by making these kinds of appointments. 1 suggest as well that we look very seriously at the fact that access to our courts is becoming increasingly restricted. This is the result of serious but-backs in legal aid programs all across Canada. This has the effect of creating a justice system in which there is full accessibility only to those who can afford to go before the courts. We in this Party have always spoken out strongly for full and equal access to the courts. I suggest it is incumbent upon both the federal and provincial Governments to provide all necessary resources to ensure that legal aid programs, both

October 11, 1985
The Governor General's Act
civil and criminal, are adequately funded. They are not adequately funded today and that can very easily lead to a system in which there is justice for the rich but not for the poor.
The Minister of Justice touched upon in particular the question of appointments of women. While some progress has been made, I think it is only appropriate to draw to the attention of this House and Canadians the fact that until this Government came into power not one woman had been appointed by a Conservative Government in the history of Canada. Not one woman by any Conservative Government since 1867. That is a pretty disgraceful record. However, 1 am pleased to note that the Government has started, albeit slowly, to appoint more women to the federal bench. However, I suggest there is no shortage of qualified women at this point and if ever there were a need for strong and effective affirmative action, it is in this area. The time has come for qualified and capable women to be appointed to the federal bench and I hope the rate of such appointments will increase very significantly.
In conclusion, I want to again emphasize the importance of the task now before Parliament in being called upon to determine an appropriate level of compensation for members of the federal judiciary. At the same time I want to underscore our concern that judges should not be appointed on the basis of how much money they are going to be making. They should be appointed on their willingness to serve and accept this very important position. In many ways there can be no greater honour for a member of the bar than to be called upon to serve as a member of the judiciary. It is a difficult job and one which by and large in this country is done very well. I know that most of us who are members of the legal profession in British Columbia have the greatest confidence in and respect for our federally-appointed judges at all levels. I think it is important that we take the opportunity, when this Bill gets to committee, to look very carefully at some of the questions raised today regarding appointments to the federal judiciary and access to the courts, and look very seriously at whether it is an appropriate time for us to be increasing salaries of judges at the federal level as proposed by this Government. We in this Party are opposing this Bill at second reading and I know my colleagues will be taking an opportunity to speak at greater length today and in the days which lie ahead.

Mr. Speaker, I see that this Bill is not going through today but that will not be on my account because I am going to finish my remarks before four o'clock. I am not going to involve myself in the argument as to whether or not a judge can scrimp by on the present salary of $95,000 and whether he really needs that extra $10,000 at a time when others in society are being asked to cut back on their expectations. I am not going to involve myself in the argument about whether or not the general level of compensation in the legal profession is too high in relation to other people in society for the type of work they do. What I am going to do is speak specifically about Clause 6 in the Bill which deals with the removal allowances paid to judges in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. There is a good reason why
you need that allowance. Judges in those jurisdictions usually come from elsewhere. However, I would like to point out that this only applies to judges who are originally from and retire to one of the 10 provinces. It occurs to me that there might well be a case where a judge originally from the Yukon goes to the Northwest Territories, or the reverse, and he or she ought to be entitled to the same removal allowance as judges originating in and returning to the south.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   INDIAN AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING INDIAN SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am delighted to rise this afternoon on behalf of the constituents of Nepean-Carleton to provide Members of the House with my analysis of the Private Members' motion which is before us. I think we all want to compliment our colleague, the Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) for his interest in native peoples, many of whom live in northern Canada and many of whom are his constituents. He has approached this subject in the House with a great deal of sincerity and integrity and he is to be complimented on that. I took the time today to read his speech of December 4 in the House when he introduced this motion. He ended his presentation that day by noting that these very important, sensitive, and difficult issues have to be addressed. I compliment him for that.
As I look at his motion which we are considering today I see that the Member for Cochrane-Superior is asking the Government to consider promoting Indian self-government by taking action in specified areas. Indian self-government, as I understand it, is intended to do the following four things: to enhance community control and decision-making; to recognize the diverse needs, traditions and cultures of those it serves; to enable Indian people to provide for Governments accountable to them rather than to the federal bureaucracy; and to establish future economic self-reliance for Indian people.
Aboriginal peoples have a historical view of this land prior to European exploration and colonization. It was inhabited by many different indigenous people who came from various geographic areas and eventually inhabited North America. These people were organized into political entities and groupings based on common language, culture, and history. These diverse communities were self-sufficient. Their economies were based variously on hunting, fishing, agriculture, gathering, and trading. Those economies depended upon the climate, forest cover, availability of game and good fishing, etc.
Over the years our native peoples were segregated onto reserve lands. The evolution of technology, the development of economies based upon manufactured products, and the dissemination of the tribes through disease disabled their traditional economic system. Many of these problems relate back to the Indian Act of 1876. Through the treaty-making process the Indians believed that their economic base would be protected or enhanced. Non-Indians saw the treaties as an extinguishment of Indian rights with the acceptance of a defined land base and government programs such as education and medical services.
Over the years various Governments have tried to stimulate economic growth in the aboriginal community. There have been some notable successes witnessed in many communities. The failures occur mainly because we have tried to impose our concept of business practices and economies on to the native peoples. The statistics tell the story. On every count aboriginal people suffered by comparison with the rest of Canadian society, even in comparison to adjacent non-native communi-

October 11, 1985
Indian Self-Government
ties. They have less education, live in lower standard housing, and suffer from more health problems. This all leads to a continuous cycle of poverty and dependence, a cycle which this Government is anxious for those peoples to break out of. Changes in the economic prospects of aboriginal people will not come about easily. Movement must take place on a number of fronts simultaneously. This will not happen overnight, but we are starting now.
To be more specific, the educational levels of native peoples have historically been less than that of non-natives. Forty-four per cent of the Indian population have less than grade nine education compared to 22 per cent of the rest of the population. Fortunately, there are some signs of change in this area. A significantly larger number of young Indians are achieving higher levels of education than were achieved in their parents' generation. Enrolment in post-secondary schools, especially in management, administrative and related programs, between 1979 and 1983 increased by 63 per cent. Enrolment in architectural, engineering and related programs in 1982 to 1984 increased four times over that in 1979 and 1980.
The view of Indian people, which view the Government supports, is that economic development is linked to self-government. I am confident that the Member for Cochrane-Superior would agree with this hypothesis. Both are necessary to achieve the common goal of increased self-reliance. Therefore, we are moving in the direction of economic control being transferred to Indian peoples. Because of the diversity of the Indian nations, a wide range of possibilities must be and will be accommodated. This takes time.
We are currently working on a number of initiatives which will assist Indian people in breaking their dependency cycle and in moving toward economic self-reliance and self-sufficiency.
For example, in confirmation of the Government's commitment to improve the quality of life of Indian people through economic development, we have announced a $24 million fund for an Indian community human resource development strategy program. This program is based on the principle that a successful human resource strategy must be tailored to the needs of the community. Communities will be encouraged to assume full responsibility for the development and implementation of their own strategies.
In July it was announced that a fund of $11 million would be made available for the implementation of the Indian fisherman's economic development program designed to stabilize the participation levels of Metis people in the West Coast fishing industry.
We are currently working in close co-operation with the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion to pursue, through various tripartite agreements with the provinces and native people, the development of specific program initiatives that take into account the needs and circumstances of native communities. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) has announced that he is exploring a means of introducing new funding arrangements for Indian bands and tribal councils. Such funding arrangements would enable them to decide how best to meet their people's needs and to set their own priorities in view of their local conditions.
The need for other changes is fully recognized. As has been said before, we must find a way in these times of restraint and fiscal responsibility to provide a level of funding sufficient so that First Nation's communities can receive levels of service on a par with other Canadians in other parts of Canada which will allow them to become healthy and productive communities. This can only be done when funds can be expended in accord with their own values and under their own control.
The economic revitalization of this country is a major goal of the Government. This revitalization is clearly needed for our aboriginal people as well as for other citizens. The Government has made a commitment that Canada's native peoples will be part of the process of building a national economic consensus. It is absolutely essential that we provide an environment in which our native peoples find their true role in our society. We want them to enhance their educational opportunities in their own communities, to enhance their social opportunities, their business interests and their total well-being so that they can contribute in their own way and in their fullest way to the fabric of Canadian society.
We have a great deal to do in working for them. Naturally, we want them to work within their own councils. Beyond that, however, they must take their place in the framework of our great Confederation. I believe it is the hope of every Member of the House and every Canadian that as we move through the 1980s we will be able to enhance the economic and social well-being of native peoples who have such a great tradition and form such a great part of Canadian and North American heritage.
The Government is looking for new approaches to replace the policies that have failed our native people so badly in the past. It is talking to aboriginal peoples and seeking their views. I know that we can succeed in establishing the new relationship that is so vital to the enhancement of their place in our society. Together we can make a better future for native persons.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking briefly in this debate, I want to make it clear that our Party supports this resolution. It aligns itself very well with the aspirations and needs of Indian people. The resolution begins by calling upon the Government to make an affirmative policy of constitutional recognition of aboriginal rights and points out that the Government could accomplish a great deal through a bilateral process of negotiation with First Nations' government. Finally, it indicates that the Government should be introducing legislation that would recognize First Nations' self-government.
My Party and I support this resolution because it brings these aspirations and hopes of aboriginal peoples directly to the attention of the Government. While it will not be easy,
October 11, 1985

Indian self-government will be achieved. I hope that we take many steps toward that goal during our lifetime.
Indian self-government must be achieved because it is the lack of self-government and self-determination which has caused native people to end up at the bottom of the totem pole. The inability of the Indian people and Indian communities to make decisions about their needs and find solutions to their problems has resulted in low levels of education in Indian communities, high levels of alcoholism, violence and extremely high unemployment. Present conditions are enough reason to move toward Indian self-government.
History will show that the symptoms of today's conditions began when their right to self-determination was taken away. When European people first stepped foot on this continent in an attempt to establish communities here, it was the Indian people who came to their aid and taught them the ways to survive on this continent. There was greater equality later on during the fur trade between the trappers and merchants. At that time there was a mutually beneficial relationship between the Indians and European people. This mutually beneficial relationship between European and native people on this continent has been destroyed as a result of the undermining of the traditional native economy and the changing political process which left Indian political organizations with very little power or influence.
We must recognize that Indian self-government is the proper solution. Canadians were made aware of this fact by the parliamentary committee which produced the report on Indian self-government entitled "Indian Self-government in Canada: A Report of the Special Committee of the House of Commons". My colleague, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), who was the chairman of that committee, deserves special recognition.
He and the other members of the committee deserve special recognition. They spoke and listened to Indian leaders right across the country. When they wrote their report, they demonstrated that they had in fact listened because the report reflected something that had been said by Indian people for many years: quite simply, that if there is going to be any real resolution to the problems that face Indian people, it is the Indian people who are going to have to fashion and implement the solution. The way to assure that that can be done by structuring the political process in a way that allows Indian people self-government.
In a country like Canada which in the past has been traumatized by threats of separatist movements, notions like self-government can throw fear into the hearts of many. It is necessary for Canadians to appreciate the need for self-government and what is meant by self-government and to appreciate that it is possible to negotiate self-government and still maintain a national unity.
I would like to pay particular tribute to those Hon. Members who served on the special parliamentary committee and issued the report on Indian self-government because they
Indian Self-Government
demonstrated that Parliament can serve a useful, worthwhile function and that it can take hold of a complex and difficult problem which has been unsolvable throughout the last 100 years of our history and come up with intelligent, reasonable and workable solutions. Having demonstrated that Parliament can work, we now need a real demonstration that Government can work.
It is not only Indian people who are cynical about the Government. In large measure, the whole of the Canadian public is cynical about the Government because Governments have so often promised so much and delivered so little. This matter provides a real opportunity for the Government of the day to live up to its promise and to demonstrate that Governments can serve people.
The cynicism that exists in the Indian community is based upon painful experience and has resulted in the fact that while this report on Indian self-government came from the Indian community, a number of Indian people have opposed its recommendations and concepts primarily because they no longer trust the political process and public authority. They feel that anything that comes from a parliamentary or Government source is bound to be flawed and detrimental to the interests of the Indian community. We have a long way to go toward building the trust that must exist between the Canadian Government and Indian communities in order to allow the negotiations that will result in Indian self-government.
There is some value to going through the agony, trouble and work that would be involved in establishing Indian self-government in this country. By achieving Indian self-government, we could aid human dignity. That Indian people face the conditions they do today is an affront to human dignity. By negotiating Indian self-government, we would show that we are no longer willing to tolerate the kinds of social and economic conditions under which Indian people live and that we would no longer tolerate the affront to human dignity that those conditions represent.
The benefits of Indian self-government would accrue not only to Indian people. Certainly Indian self-government would lead to a better life for Indian people and it would lead to the development of Indian communities and individuals. As well, it would be of benefit to the entire nation because as one segment of the community flourishes, we all benefit. As one flower in the garden blossoms, the beauty of the entire garden is enhanced.
As we demonstrate that it is possible for this nation to negotiate and create Indian self-government, a measure of democracy, we could also extend that same kind of negotiation in other directions. There are many other communities in this country that feel powerless and are cynical about the promise of democracy. If we could demonstrate that we are capable of putting in place a democratic system for Indian people, then we could do that with regard to other groups and communities as well.
The resolution brought forward by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior is a historic resolution. It is a real step forward in the progress of the Indian people of this country

October 11, 1985
Indian Self-Government
and in the building of national unity. I would call upon the Government to take very seriously the concept of Indian self-government and to seek all ways possible to achieve it in reality without simply speaking of it in rhetorical terms.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by congratulating the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) on the interest he has shown here today for our native communities, an interest that was apparent before, both in the proceedings of the parliamentary committee and in this House. The Hon. Member may be aware that my riding too has a native population that is very much present, very community-oriented, and that also wants to evolve towards a certain form of self-determination.
In the motion presented by the Hon. Member, he is asking the Government to support the adoption of an affirmative policy of constitutional recognition of aboriginal self-government. In this respect, Mr. Speaker, I would like to recall, first of all, that at the First Ministers' Conference on constitutional issues concerning native peoples, held on April 2 and 3, 1985, the Government indicated that it was entirely in favour of adopting a Bill to amend the Constitution, to recognize and affirm the right of aboriginal peoples to self-government within the Canadian confederation.
In his preliminary speech, the Prime Minister indicated that, like other Canadians, Indians, Inuit and Metis must be able to take responsibility for their own affairs by setting their own priorities and establishing their own programs. They also must have a guarantee that their cultural and linguistic background and traditions will be respected. "The key to the changes that are necessary . .." said the Prime Minister, " ... is to grant (native people) self-government within the Canadian confederation".
Mr. Speaker, he also recognized and accepted the desire of native peoples to have their rights, which are unique, enshrined in the supreme law of the land, in order to protect these rights against any legislative interference. The federal Government has demonstrated its commitment to providing constitutional protection for native rights in the amending proposal tabled at the conference, in which we find the following elements:
The recognition and affirmation of the right of native peoples to self-government within the Canadian confederation, provided these rights are set forth in agreements negotiated and approved by the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislative assemblies concerned;
Second, a commitment by the federal and provincial governments to conducting negotiations with native peoples on the issue of self-government, in accordance with their respective
jurisdictions, while providing for participation by territorial governments if necessary.
I am sure I do not have to remind Hon. Members that the Constitution Act, 1982, contains a constitutional amending formula requiring the agreement of two-thirds of the provinces whose total population is equal to at least half of the population of the country. Furthermore, Section 37 of the Constitution Act provides for participation by representatives of the Indians, Inuit and Metis, and of both territories, in the process of determining native rights.
Obviously, it is not easy to reach an agreement when there are so many parties with such vastly diverging interests. However, the federal Government, by playing the role of moderator as well as tabling a detailed and innovative amending proposal, has helped to create the requisite framework for discussion and reaching an acceptable compromise.
The initial reaction of native participants was that although the amending proposal did not go far enough, considering the provisions they wanted to see in the Constitution, it was nevertheless a good starting point for discussion.
Among the provinces, reactions varied from unqualified support for the federal Government's proposal to outright rejection. The proposal was supported by five provinces: Ontario, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan admitted that it responded to many of their concerns. However, Nova Scotia would have preferred a more precise definition of self-government, while Saskatchewan was concerned about the nature of commitments that were not clearly defined and the risk of court challenges. British Columbia and Alberta were opposed to the proposal. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Cros-bie), who played a major role at the Constitutional Conference, chaired meetings held in camera on the evening of the first day and the following morning, in an attempt to try and develop a constitutional amending proposal that would be acceptable to all parties. The struggle to find a common ground that would make it possible to reach a compromise was a long and difficult one.
The federal Government's new proposal, reflecting Saskatchewan's compromise, was tabled around noon on the second day. It differed from the initial proposal in that, first of all, the commitment concerning the negotiating process was withdrawn from the amending proposal and included in the agreement. Second, the approval of the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislative assemblies concerned would be necessary to conclude any agreement on self-government. Third, a provision was added to the amending proposal to protect native people against any measure that would repeal of infringe on their rights, including their rights to self-government.
The new provisions of the Accord included, among other things, the right to appear before the First Ministers' conference and present progress reports on the negotiations as well as

proposed amendments to the Constitution with respect to self-government, an item which was to be on the agenda of the following conference of First Ministers on constitutional matters concerning aboriginal peoples.
This new proposition gave rise to various reactions from the provinces and the organizations of aboriginal peoples, from rejection in certain cases-because it did not go far enough- to conditional acceptance in other cases.
British Columbia tabled a counterproposition. Some provinces stated they would not take position until the aboriginal groups had expressed their views, and the Inuit Committee on National Issues said it would announce its opinion only after further consultations with other Inuit people. The Native Council of Canada and the Metis National Council both expressed conditional support for the new proposition, whereas the Assembly of First Nations rejected it outright even though it endorsed the initiative taken by the Government.
Just so the representatives would have time to consult with their aboriginal brothers, more ministerial meetings were held last June 6 and 7 to continue the discussions. At the time the federal Government indicated its willingness to support any proposition deemed acceptable to the other parties.
However it soon became obvious that it would be impossible to reach an immediate consensus to adopt a proposed amendment.
We were disappointed but not discouraged by the outcome, if only because it had been possible to reach agreement on more issues than ever before. What matters now is to provide unequivocal evidence that self-government is a viable concept in Canada. The constitutional process is therefore still ongoing as we wait for the 1987 conference.
In the meantime, mechanisms other than the constitutional process are being set up to show that the Government does indeed take the necessary steps in this field.
Earlier, the Hon. Member mentioned a host of programs that have been made available to native peoples and should be seen as a transitional measure, to help them until such time as native rights can again be enshrined in the Constitution.
However, I believe that the federal Government's commitment to recognition of aboriginal self-government in the Constitution has been made abundantly clear, and that is why we are asking all Canadians to give their elected representatives the support they need to enact this draft amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments this afternoon particularly on the motion and generally on the question of Indian self-government. I should like to begin by being as partisan as I am going to be in this debate and by paying tribute to the Hon. Member who moved this motion, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner). If a certain Prime Minister in a previous Government had been more
Indian Self-Government
well-intentioned in his thinking, he would have named this Member as the Minister of Indian Affairs, and a great number of the difficulties encountered by Indian people would not have been encountered to the extent that they were. I pay tribute to him for his invaluable work both on the subcommittee report on self-government and for his continuing work in the House of Commons. He deserves our thanks.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   INDIAN AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING INDIAN SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   INDIAN AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING INDIAN SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I feel qualified in some respects to speak about Indian self-government, in that my constituency of The Battlefords-Meadowlake has some 19 Indian reservations. Approximately 22 per cent of the electors or citizens in my constituency are of native ancestry. These people feel very strongly about the need for self-government and are supportive in principle of the move of our Government as it continues toward genuine native self-government.
As was mentioned by the previous Hon. Member who spoke, many interpretations were given, at the First Ministers' meeting and at other conferences, about what precisely was selfgovernment. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) is working with a large number of native constituencies, provincial Governments and other native organizations toward specifically defining self-government. However, the general principle is one which I think all Hon. Members of the House can support, to the extent that the Minister has been working hard to bring self-government to reality.
There is a historical need for Indian self-government. The very principle of a Government ending the 20th century with a specific Department which deals with the running of people's lives, namely the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, is no longer acceptable. There is no doubt that that institution has long passed its time. A very necessary, historical point must be mentioned first-the native people of Canada must be the people who control their own destiny. For that reason it is crucial for us to move toward the position of self-government and to continue to move at a rate which will see the Hon. Minister, as he said, as the last Minister of Indian Affairs. This is his desire. I think it is the desire of all Members of this House.
I had the opportunity to speak recently to a native economic development conference. I spoke at that time about the need to couple the move to self-government with many other areas of concern of native people. Economic development is the most prominent of those concerns, of course, and this is being acknowledged by native people in my constituency of The Battlefords-Meadow Lake as a movement away from what they have seen, within the framework of this very paternalistic Department of Indian Affairs mechanism, as a hand-out mentality. When they look back on the years of reliance on the Department of Indian Affairs they see that economic development has not worked. Quite simply, the approach of the Government in handing out amounts of money to people.

October 11, 1985
Indian Self-Government
perpetuating a sense of reliance on the Government, is a system which is doomed to fail. These native investors and businessmen and businesswomen now see economic development as a self-sustained, self-driving sort of entrepreneurship. These people see that genuine economic development will only come as native people begin to govern themselves.
The process of devolution of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and of many of the other roles that the federal Government plays is a request long held by native people in my constituency. Presently across the spending range of the Government of Canada there is almost $3 billion annually spent through 11 different Government Departments on native people and native programs. Understandably the native community and the non-native taxpaying community share many of the same frustrations, and the frustration quite simply is, are we getting value for our money? I don't mean this as an aspersion upon the urban community of Canada but I travel to larger Canadian cities and I do sense there is a very profound misunderstanding of the way in which funds are administered to native peoples.
One only need drive, as I do, thousands of miles a year from reserve to reserve to see that with a consistency that is alarming, and I use the word shocking, that native people have a standard of health that is below that of non-native more urbanized Canadians; a standard of education that is lower and certainly a standard of housing which is sub-standard. The taxpayer says the Government is spending almost $3 billion a year on all of these programs so surely the native people must be getting at least enough money, if not more than that which they are entitled to. That is not true, Mr. Speaker. One only needs to see the standard of living in those Indian reservations and it will be obvious that the money is not finding its way to the rightful people who should be benefiting from that money, namely the Indian men, women and children of Canada.
There is a latent frustration, which is coming ever more to the surface, by the native community, saying that band by band, local Indian community by Indian community these people are not able to enjoy a standard of living in the commitment that the Government of Canada has made to them.
On the other hand, the taxpaying non-native person says, how much more money should the Government be spending. The answer is clear that a great deal of this money is lost, if I may use that term, in administration. Of the vast mechanism that we call the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, administration within the native community in the very large native umbrella organizations is not, in my humble opinion, representing the aspirations, the desires, the goals, the ideals of the average person on the reserve as well as the local chief and council, or the local tribal council or district chiefs association would be representating their concerns.
We have two large mechanisms within the native community first and, second, within the Department of Indian Affairs that on an administrative basis are consuming vast amounts of money and I think not providing the service to native people that could be provided at their own grass roots level.
The answer is clearly to begin to devolve this process and move toward genuine self-government. A system of self-government as I would envisage it would see the political, the economic and the economic development opportunity resting with those people who best know their community. The local chiefs, the tribal councils, the organizations of district chiefs are the groups that know about the true needs in the native community and are better set to administer it politically and certainly, an important aspect, financially.
If one looks at the present move toward self-government I think that we should pay tribute for a moment to the present Minister. I cannot speak with any scientific accuracy, but certainly by the experience of watching the Minister travel, he has logged more miles than many Ministers in the Department of Indian Affairs have done in the past. An important aspect of what our Minister has done is this concern that he has shown for the local band, the local native community. I know in my Province of Saskatchewan where we have 69 Indian bands we have seen this Minister visit the province several times in his first year of office, and that first year is a difficult time for any Minister. The Minister made this endeavour to talk with native people in individual bands in their own communities.
An Hon. Member speaking earlier mentioned the First Ministers' Conference on Native Affairs and Indian Self-Government and the disappointment felt by our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who came closer than any Minister has come in the past as a First Minister to secure a specific commitment on behalf of the Governments of Canada to entrenching the need for self-government in the Constitution.
The Prime Minister, the Minister of Indian Affairs, their colleague the Minister of Health have all spoken clearly for the need to have Indian people control their own destinies, and I think that is a tribute to what this Government is doing.
As a Member in the last session of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development I had the honour to work extensively on Bill C-31 which was a historic day for native women and for those who had lost their status as treaty Indian people. This was a Bill that, like self-government, had long been desired. It has been talked about for a long time. I think it is significant that it is the first major piece of legislation by which the Minister of Indian Affairs chose to right a historic wrong that affected our native people.
I know there are other Members who would like to speak today so I will wind up my remarks by saying that the move to self-government is truly upon us. It makes sense, first and most importantly, for the native communities. Like any people who aspire to control their own destiny are well deserving-I should not use the term right, it was a right long ago for people to control their own lives-but, for lack of a better word, these people are now ready. They want that right to be able to control their own lives and their own communities.
The larger question of responsibility also rests with the native people who say they want full responsibility for housing, education, economic development and health. These are matters that should no longer be administered from afar by a large
October 11, 1985

weighty Government bureaucracy. Similarly there is a feeling I think in the rest of Canada that self-government is a proposal that will begin to give true autonomy to the native community and therefore a more efficient use of not only the funds but the expertise and the political development between the Government of Canada and the Governments of first nations. I fully applaud our Minister of Indian Affairs for undertaking the initiative that he has thus far and I know that he will have the support of all Members of the House as he moves toward constitutional self-government and the areas of non-constitutional self-government. I know that all Members will join with me in supporting our government's proposals, our government's move and push towards full self-government for native people.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   INDIAN AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING INDIAN SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin, with permission of the House, by congratulating the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Gorm-ley), who has just spoken, for a thoughtful, well informed and sensitive discussion of what is a very, very important issue. I also think it is exceedingly important, as those who have preceded me, to comment upon the dedication of the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) for whom this has been an interest and a concern-perhaps even a mission- for many, many years. It is largely to his credit that the issue is before us now. I know that all Members of the House recognize the contribution of an individual Member and, quite frankly, I think what the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior has demonstrated to us is the ability of a so-called back-bencher, a so-called ordinary Member of the House of Commons, to make a significant contribution. He is to be commended. I think many of us hope to use him as a model in the years to come.
The issue which is before us is an important one. Yet, in many ways it is a difficult one, particularly for those Canadians who have not had the opportunity to have any type of direct and intimate experience with the Canadian Indian community. 1 have had a reasonably close association within the community in two ways for which I am pleased. First, as a Canadian historian, and although I do not pretend to be an expert in Canadian Indian history, I have paid a considerable amount of attention to the history of the Canadian Indians and their relationship with other Canadians. Second, I have had the distinction in the past to have taught a number of Indian students at the university level in the early 1960s when many of our education programs for Canadian Indians at the university level were just beginning.
I became very aware at that point in time, as a result of that experience, of some of the tremendous difficulties faced by young and not so young Canadian Indians who were seeking to improve upon their own economic and educational positions. I became aware as I visited them in their reserves and taught them in their own northern communities of the incredible disadvantages which they faced and of which many other Canadians were largely unaware.
Indian Self-Government
I would like to take this opportunity to share with the Members of the House one of my first intimate experiences with a young Indian lad. I think he was probably about 18 at the time. He had been brought to the college residence where 1 happened to be the Dean. This chap was trying to break new ground by continuing on in an educational program at a time when he was very much a part of a minority. He was trying to finish his high school. Unfortunately, there were no others within that high school community who were of Indian ancestry. This young person who had been supported by the President of Brandon College, as it then was, and which is now Brandon University, had been selected because he had remarkable artistic talents. He was doing well as a high school scholar. Unfortunately, to my dismay, he did not return from the Christmas vacation.
Because I had grown fond of this young man, whose name is Cecil, I went to seek him out in his home. That was my first real genuine introduction to the living conditions to which other Members have referred. I found him in a cabin not too far from Portage La Prairie in the Province of Manitoba. 1 found him with some difficulty because he was living with his grandmother. I went and spoke to him about why he should return to school and why he should make his contribution.
It seems to me that the goal of self government, the topic which we are addressing today, is to a large degree dependent upon the likes of Cecil attaining an education and assuming a role of leadership within the native community. Cecil was reluctant to talk about why he had not come back to the residence and to school. We sat in the kitchen of the two-room cabin and I, with all the enthusiasm and naivete of a 27-year old white Canadian who knew little of what he was talking about, tried to explain to this young man how important it was for him to carry on with his education. Cecil did not talk a great deal. However, he finally said that he wanted to come back but there were many reasons why he could not. He explained to me that he was there to chop wood. He was chopping the wood because there was no one else in his family who was able to chop it in order to keep the fires lit. This was the month of January, although I have forgotten the year. His sisters and brothers had been and were being raised by his grandmother who was ill and not present at the time. Neither his father nor mother were available to carry on with their parental responsibilities. Thus, young Cecil, who wished to be an artist and to become educated like other white Canadians, who wished to play a role in society, felt that his responsibilities as an elder member of the family required him to drop out of school and return home.
We talked and talked for a long time. I even reached the point where I offered to help cut the wood, although that was obviously a short-term solution. What he finally did was bring me a poem which he had written. The poem was about a young Indian lad who had a brother. The brother had become ill. The family in the poem lived on the reserve, which is certainly a tragic by-product in many ways of our Canadian history. The brother in the poem had tried to get some help for his younger brother who was seriously ill. He had called a doctor by

October 11, 1985
Indian Self-Government
walking to a phone since there was no telephone in the home. The doctor would not come to the reserve. The only solution was for the young Indian lad in the poem to take his sick brother to the doctor, which he began to do, according to the story outlined in the poem. It was wintertime and he trudged across the snow-covered fields of Manitoba carrying his ailing brother in search of medical assistance.
As I read to the bottom of the poem the story revealed that the young brother had died in the arms of the older brother. After I had finished reading the poem I looked up at Cecil who was sitting there in the cabin with me. After a few moments of hesitation he said to me that he was the elder brother in the poem. He had given me his own autobiography. As I thought about what I had read I realized just how inadequate my own comprehension was of the lot of the life which that young individual faced.
I realize that when we talk about the history of the Canadian Indian who lives on the reserve and when we look at some of the statistics we find it exceedingly difficult, perhaps impossible, to fully realize the incredible barrier experienced by such Canadians.
Cecil came back to college, although I am not sure whether he finished his high school education. I do know that he went on and participated in some of the other Government programs
that were available. I see him from time to time when I am home in my riding. Today, he is an ordinary Canadian. He lives not too far from the constituency which I represent. I see him in the City of Brandon. He has a family and is self-supporting. He will not be a person of any particular distinction because I think he has failed to develop his artistic skills. However, he is carrying on as a self-supporting Canadian citizen.
It seems to me that what we are attempting to do and what we are hoping will happen is that people such as Cecil, who were in many ways victims of a highly paternalistic governmental system developed in Canada after the 1870s, and particularly after the tragic event of the 1885 rebellion, will slowly but surely evolve to recover the concepts of self-government and self-sufficiency.
When the whites first arrived the Canadian Indians were a self-governing people. I look forward to the day when they will return to that same position.
